metaData.originalTitle: 刚刚，一篇最全 Agent Harness 综述来了！
metaData.title: Just In: The Most Comprehensive Agent Harness Overview Yet
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically reviews the concept of Agent Harness Engineering, its seven-layer framework (ETCLOVG), and engineering evolution, emphasizing that the engineering shell outside the model is key to moving Agents from demos to production.
metaData.summary: This article provides an in-depth interpretation of a survey paper on Agent Harness jointly published by institutions including CMU, Yale, and JHU. It points out that the current bottleneck in Agent research has shifted from model capabilities to the engineering system outside the model, namely the Agent Harness. The authors propose the ETCLOVG seven-layer framework, covering Execution Environment, Tool Interface, Context Management, Lifecycle Orchestration, Observability, Validation and Evaluation, and Safety and Governance. The article outlines three major engineering migrations from Prompt Engineering to Context Engineering to Harness Engineering, and emphasizes that observability and governance are independent core layers for production-grade Agents. It also discusses cross-layer issues such as the cost-quality-speed triangle and the capability-control paradox, noting that competition among Agent platforms will revolve around the complete set of Harness capabilities. Finally, the article reminds that Harness design should dynamically adjust as model capabilities evolve, avoiding over-scaffolding.

mainPoints.point: The performance bottleneck of Agents is shifting from model capabilities to the engineering system (Harness) outside the model.
mainPoints.explanation: The paper points out that in long-horizon tasks with real-world tools, Agent failures often stem from poor system management rather than insufficient model intelligence. Improving the Harness can yield multiple-fold performance gains without changing the model.

mainPoints.point: Agent engineering has undergone three migrations: from Prompt Engineering to Context Engineering to Harness Engineering.
mainPoints.explanation: Prompt Engineering addresses how to talk to the model, Context Engineering addresses what the model should see, and Harness Engineering addresses how to make the model act reliably in the real world.

mainPoints.point: The ETCLOVG seven-layer framework is a systematic guide for building production-grade Agents.
mainPoints.explanation: This framework covers Execution Environment, Tool Interface, Context Management, Lifecycle Orchestration, Observability, Validation and Evaluation, and Safety and Governance. Together, these seven layers form a complete Agent system capable of handling long-horizon tasks.

mainPoints.point: Observability and governance are independent core layers of production-grade Agents, not auxiliary features.
mainPoints.explanation: When an Agent performs real-world operations, it must know what it has done (observability) and what it is allowed to do (governance); otherwise, it is impossible to diagnose failures or ensure safety and control.

mainPoints.point: Agent evaluation should shift from final success rates to trace-native evaluation based on complete execution trajectories.
mainPoints.explanation: Final success rates obscure the influence of multiple variables such as models, prompts, tools, and context. Trace-native evaluation records the complete execution trajectory to assess result correctness, path rationality, and evaluator reliability.

keyQuotes: The same model, with a different execution shell, can perform completely differently.

Prompt Engineering addresses 'how to talk to the model.' Context Engineering addresses 'what the model should see.' Harness Engineering addresses 'how to make the model work reliably in the real world.'
The next competition for Agents is not just about model capabilities, but the engineering shell outside the model.
A good Harness not only knows how to add controls, but also when to remove them.
For Agents to evolve from toys to infrastructure, this shell is exactly what is missing.

relatedArticles.title: Harness Engineering is Taking Silicon Valley by Storm: A Deep Dive!
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of the popular Silicon Valley concept of 'Harness Engineering,' proposing the formula 'Agent = Model + Harness,' and emphasizes unleashing AI productivity by building structured environments, feedback loops, and evaluation systems.

relatedArticles.title: Latest! A 10,000-Word Overview of the Harness Revolution!
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Based on the AI development context of 2026, this article systematically elaborates on Agent Harness as a strategic infrastructure for managing the complexity of agents. Starting from the evolution of software engineering history, it analyzes its core components and ecosystem landscape, and explores the direction of engineers' capability transformation in the Agent era.

relatedArticles.title: Designing a Production-Grade Multi-Agent Harness from Scratch: Architecture, Evaluation, Memory, Cost, and MCP Tool Integration
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically deconstructs the design principles and engineering practices of a production-grade Multi-Agent Harness, covering architecture orchestration, tool governance, state and memory, evaluation systems, cost control, and MCP integration.

relatedArticles.title: MiniMax M2.7: Unlocking Model Self-Evolution
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: MiniMax releases the M2.7 model, featuring 'model self-evolution' capabilities and achieving significant breakthroughs in software engineering, professional office productivity, and multi-agent collaboration.

relatedArticles.title: What MiniMax Truly Aims For Is the Dual Evolution of Models and Harness!
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article, through analyzing the live discussion between MiniMax and the Hermes Agent team and the hands-on experience with MaxHermes, delves into the trend of AI Agents evolving from single-turn Q&A to continuous workflows, and proposes the core viewpoint of 'the collaborative evolution of models and Harness'.

relatedArticles.title: Build a 24/7 AI Team with OpenClaw: A Practical Guide!
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A Senior AI Product Manager at Google shares how to build a highly efficient and cost-effective 6-person AI Agent automation team using the OpenClaw framework through persona definition, file system collaboration, and a dual-layer memory mechanism.

relatedArticles.title: Is Your AI Agent Truly Under Control?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Taking OpenClaw as an example, this article systematically explains how to build an observability system for AI Agents using session audit logs, application logs, and OTEL telemetry, to address the challenges of security and controlled operation caused by their non-deterministic behavior.

relatedArticles.title: On Agent Memory
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article delves into the essence, architectural philosophy, and governance challenges of AI Agent memory systems, arguing that true memory is not simple storage and retrieval, but the continuous reinterpretation, hierarchical governance, and skill solidification of past experiences, while critiquing the common misconception of equating RAG or long context with memory.

relatedArticles.title: Lessons Learned from Building Claude Code Revealed for the First Time!
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Anthropic team members reveal the tool design principles of Claude Code for the first time, advocating that tools should evolve with model capabilities and emphasizing letting Agents autonomously build context to optimize their action space.

relatedArticles.title: Exploring Claude Code: Understanding Agent Harness | A Conversation with Xinlu Lai
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: An in-depth analysis of the engineering practices behind Agent Harness, using Claude Code's source code as a specimen to explore its three-layer architecture (execution, context, governance) and the ingenious design of memory and context management.
